'''''Delairea odorata''''' is a [[vine|climber]] within the family [[Asteraceae]] that is native to [[South Africa]]. One of the two species in the genus ''[[Delairea]]'' (the other being ''[[Delairea aparadensis]]''), it was previously included in the genus ''[[Senecio]]'' as '''''Senecio mikanioides'''''.<ref>{{Cite web
 |last         = Eda
 |first        = Sayaka
 |title        = The Biogeography of Cape Ivy (''Delairea odorata'')
 |year         = 1999
 |url          = http://bss.sfsu.edu/holzman/courses/Fall99Projects/capeivy.htm
 |access-date   = 2007-05-20
 |url-status      = dead
 |archive-url   = https://web.archive.org/web/20070513074213/http://bss.sfsu.edu/holzman/courses/Fall99Projects/capeivy.htm
 |archive-date  = 2007-05-13
}}</ref> It is known as '''Cape ivy''' in some parts of the world (US) and '''German ivy'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> in others (Britain, Ireland). Other names include '''parlor ivy''' and '''Italian ivy'''.<ref name=hear/> 

It is a twining perennial, herbaceous plant that grows {{Convert|3|m}} tall.<ref>[https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Delairea~odorata Delairea odorata Lem.] NEW SOUTH WALES FLORA ONLINE, PlantNET. G. J. Harden, 1992. Retrieved 28 March 2023.</ref> Its multi-lobed leaves somewhat resemble those of the unrelated [[English ivy]]. Originally used as an [[ornamental plant]] on [[Trellis|trellis]]es and as [[groundcover]], it is now rarely cultivated because of its [[invasive species|invasiveness]], in addition to being a [[weed]].<ref name = plantfile>[https://plantfileonline.net/plants/plant_details/42 ''Delairea odorata''] PlantFileonline</ref>  Although it resembles ''[[Senecio tamoides]]'', [[Open Tree of Life]] indicates that it is most closely related to species in the genus [[Curio (plant)|''Curio'']], followed by ''[[Senecio angulatus]]''.<ref>{{cite web 
 |title=Curio + Delairea
 |url=https://tree.opentreeoflife.org/opentree/opentree16.1@mrcaott76302ott304648/Curio--Delairea
 |website=Open Tree of Life 
 |publisher=Open Tree of Life Project 
 |access-date=2026-03-28 
}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Starr 070621-7440 Delairea odorata.jpg|thumb|left|Leaf detail]]
[[File:Delairea (Senecio Mikanioides).jpg|thumb|left|Blooms pollinated by bees]]
''Delairea odorata'' is a fast-growing vine<ref>[https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Capeivy Cape ivy (Delairea odorata)] [[Department of Planning and Environment (New South Wales)|NSW Department of Industry]]</ref> that can climb to heights of {{convert|2–4|m|ft|0}}.<ref name = plantfile/> 

The glossy and semi-[[succulent]] leaves, which are {{convert|3-10|cm|frac=4}} long and {{convert|3-8|cm|frac=4}} wide, are alternately arranged along the stems. They have 3–10 rather broad lobes. The upper leaf surface is light green, usually with a somewhat purple cast, while the reverse is somewhat silvery.<ref name = weeds>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/delairea_odorata.htm ''Delairea odorata''] Environmental Weeds of Australia</ref>

The plant's stems and leaves will die between late summer and early autumn, being superseded by new shoots that employ the old stems as climbing support.<ref>DiTomaso, J. M., Kyser, G. B., Oneto, S. R., Wilson, R. G., Orloff, S. B., Anderson, L. W., ... & Mann, J. J. (2013). Weed Report: ''Delairea odorata'' Cape-ivy In: Weed control in natural areas in the western United States. Weed Research and Information Center, University of California, 544.</ref>

===Inflorescence===
Its sweet-scented<ref>[http://www.herbiguide.com.au/Descriptions/hg_Cape_Ivy.htm Cape Ivy] Collated by HerbiGuide</ref> discoid flowers are yellow, and lack the petal-like ray [[floret]]s found in typical daisies. They have tiny tubular florets surrounded by an [[involucre]] of 8-10 small green [[phyllary|phyllaries]] ({{convert|3-5|mm|frac=128}} long). Flower-heads ({{convert|2-7|mm|frac=128}} across and {{convert|2-5|mm|frac=128}} long) occur in compact clusters at the ends of the branches (terminal [[corymbs]]), with clusters consisting of about 15-50 flower-heads. Flowering occurs mostly during winter to early spring.<ref name = weeds/> More broadly, it can flower from as early as autumn through to early spring.<ref>{{cite web |title=Delairea odorata |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/delairea_odorata.htm |website=Lucid Key Server – Plants of South East NSW |publisher=Lucidcentral |access-date=28 April 2026}}</ref>

The seeds (or [[achenes]]) are approximately {{convert|2|mm|frac=128}} long and are reddish-brown in colour, with a [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]] of silky white hairs that is {{convert|5-6|mm|frac=128}} long.<ref name = weeds/> Most of its seed in North America and possibly elsewhere is unviable, which may be due to a lack of effective [[pollinator]]s. However, the plant readily [[vegetative reproduction|reproduce]] from stem fragments, [[stolons]], or [[rhizomes]] as small as {{convert|2.5|cm|frac=128}}.<ref name="CABI-ISC">{{cite web | title=''Delairea odorata'' (Cape ivy) | website=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International|CABI]] (Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International) | date=2019-11-24 | url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/18265 | access-date=2022-06-23}}</ref>

==Habitat and distribution==
This plant is somewhat scarce in its native country of South Africa, where it was originally found in the [[Drakensberg Mountains]], on forest edges, at elevations above {{convert|1500|m}}, in [[moist forest|moist areas]]. Its presence in coastal areas (some of which are arid) in South Africa is probably more recent. In [[California]], it is generally found in the coastal fog belt, with a few specimens found inland, particularly in [[subtropical]] [[riparian]] sites that feature permanent moisture.<ref name="CABI-ISC" /> 

It is found in wetter, more temperate regions, but it may still be found in cooler subtropical environments, despite being frost tender. It prefers partial shade, but can withstand heavy shade. In cooler, damper areas, it can prosper in full sun. Despite its invasive nature, the plant is grown as an ornamental houseplant for its foliage.<ref name="CABI-ISC" /> Its active growth is from early autumn to late spring, with a [[dormancy|dormant]] period in summer.<ref>[https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/weeds-australia/profile/Delairea%20odorata Delairea odorata Lem.] WEEDS AUSTRALIA - PROFILES. Retrieved 21 May, 2023</ref> 

=== Ecological impact ===
[[File:Starr 070308-5481 Delairea odorata.jpg|240px|thumb|Covering native woodland in Hawaii]]
''D. odorata'' has been an [[invasive species]] in coastal California<ref name="Cal-IPC">{{cite web | title=''Delairea odorata'' Profile | website=[[California Invasive Plant Council]] (Cal-IPC) | date=2017-03-20 | url=http://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/delairea-odorata-profile/ | access-date=2022-06-23}}</ref><ref name="Calflora">{{cite web | title=''Delairea odorata'' | website=[[Calflora]] | url=http://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=9623 | access-date=2022-06-23}}</ref><ref name="Jepson-Herb">{{cite web | title=''Delairea odorata'' | website=[[University and Jepson Herbaria]] | date=2022-06-23 | url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=80449 | access-date=2022-06-23}}</ref><ref name="Invasive_Org">{{cite web | title=cape ivy, ''Delairea odorata'' Asterales: Asteraceae | website=[[Invasive.Org]] | url=http://www.invasive.org/browse/subinfo.cfm?sub=5529 | access-date=2022-06-23}}</ref> since 1892,<ref name="USDA-APHIS-PPQ">{{cite report | title=Weed Risk Assessment for ''Delairea odorata'' Lem. (Asteraceae) – Cape ivy | author=[[Plant Protection and Quarantine]], Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, United States Department of Agriculture | date=September 24, 2013 | url=https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Delairea_odorata_WRA.pdf}} [[Invasive Species Compendium|CABI ISC]] [http://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/20143118470 20143118470].</ref> Hawaii,<ref name="Invasive_Org" /> coastal Oregon,<ref name="Invasive_Org" /> New Zealand<ref name="Invasive_Org" /> and southern Australia<ref name="Invasive_Org" /> (particularly in Victoria). The plant will cover shrubs and trees, inhibiting growth, and will also cover ground intensively over a wide area, thereby impeding the germination and growth of native seeds. It is toxic to animals who eat it and to fish, where it trails into waterways.<ref name="Cal-IPC" /> 

''D. odorata'' reaches reproductive maturity in two years, and can produce over 30,000 seeds annually.<ref name = plantfile/> In [[Hawaii]], a purposely-introduced species of [[Arctiinae|arctiinid]] [[moth]] (''[[Galtara extensa]]''), for the biological control of ''[[Senecio madagascariensis]]'' {{endash}} both species originally from [[Madagascar]] {{endash}} proved to feed also on ''D.{{nbsp}}odorata''.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://northhawaiinews.com/sections/news/miracle-moth-madagascar.html | newspaper=[[North Hawaii News]] | title=Miracle moth from Madagascar | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141011093050/http://northhawaiinews.com/sections/news/miracle-moth-madagascar.html | archive-date=2014-10-11 | date=October 7, 2014}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Senecio mikanioides-1-bsi-yercaud-salem-India.JPG|thumb|Cultivated as a [[pot plant]] in India]]
Germany ivy is grown as a vine or groundcover, where it can vigorously climb up posts, hedges, trees and shrubs, fences, banks, and walls.<ref name=hear>[http://www.hear.org/starr/hiplants/reports/pdf/delairea_odorata.pdf Delairea odorata] Forest Starr, Kim Starr, and Lloyd Loope. United States Geological Survey--Biological Resources Division. Haleakala Field Station, Maui, Hawai'i. January, 2003.Retrieved 31 October 2022. </ref> The plant is cultivated in landscaping for its ivy-like leaves and scented flowers in bright light or light shade away from abundant sunlight. Propagation is done by [[cuttings (plants)|cuttings]] as its stems root readily both in water and soil, without the need for a [[rooting hormone]]. [[Pruning]] is encouraged for a bushy and compact growth.<ref name =home>[https://homeplantsguide.com/houseplants/senecio-mikanioides-grow-and-care.html How to grow and care for German Ivy (Senecio mikanioides) Indoors] homeplantsguide.com. Retrieved 31 October 2022.</ref>

Although it can tolerate drought, it thrives better in moist soils, but it cannot withstand soggy soils. When overwatered, its leaves turn brown and have curled edges. Conversely, underwatering will cause its leaves to fall. The plant flourishes in moister winter months and particularly after rainfalls where it displays bright green foliage. During the dry months it may die back to its stems or maintain a minimal growth.<ref name=hear/> Pests include [[mealy bug]]s and [[aphids]], and diseases include [[leaf spot]] and [[root rot]].<ref name =home/>
===History===
The plant was introduced to the United States in the 19th century as a [[Victorian era]]-style [[houseplant]].<ref name=hear/> In the 1850s, in [[Geelong]], the plant was described in the [[Geelong Advertiser]], "the great stumps, over which the little boys played [[leap-frog]], are either gone or covered with the Cape ivy". Furthermore, 1856 and 1864 [[Column (periodical)|column]]s in the [[Sydney Morning Herald]] mention a Cape Ivy observed on the dunes at [[Newcastle, New South Wales]] and [[Gulaga]].<ref name="Melbourne">{{cite web | url=https://weedsofmelbourne.org/cape-ivy-delairea-odorata | title=Cape Ivy (''Delairea odorata'') | website=Weeds of Melbourne | date=July 4, 2019}}</ref> In 1909, it was introduced as an ornamental to [[Kailua-Kona, Hawaii]]. Neal (1965) described the plant as, "both a weed and an ornamental."<ref name=hear/> 

Today it is no longer a fashionable garden plant and is a [[escaped plant|garden escape]], though it may still be found in old gardens.<ref>[https://invasives.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/sub-escaped_garden_KTP_april09B.pdf Escaped Garden Plants As A Key Threatening Processes] Invasive Species Council Australia. April 2009. Retrieved May 5 2025.</ref>

==Similar species==
German ivy is very similar to ''[[Senecio angulatus]]'', ''[[Senecio tamoides]]'' and ''[[Senecio macroglossus]]''.<ref name = weeds/> A feature that distinguishes this plant from ''Senecio angulatus'' and ''S. tamoides'' are the small ear-shaped appendages at the base of the stalks of the leaves and its pompom-like flowers which do not have obvious 'petals', whereas ''S. angulatus'' and ''S. tamoides'' have daisy-like flowers.<ref name = weeds/><ref>[https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/CapeIvy Cape ivy (Delairea odorata)] NSW WeedWise</ref> [[Atlas of Living Australia]] has misapplied ''S. tamoides'' for its ''D. odorata'' observations in Australia.<ref name="ALA">{{cite web | access-date=2022-10-19 | year=1994 | website=[[Atlas of Living Australia]] | url=https://biocache.ala.org.au/occurrences/search?q=lsid:https://id.biodiversity.org.au/node/apni/2887441&qualityProfile=ALA&qc=&wkt=MULTIPOLYGON(((150.82031249999997+-33.56318738128773,150.82031249999997%20-34.15618362669792,151.446533203125%20-34.15618362669792,151.446533203125%20-33.56318738128773,150.82031249999997%20-33.56318738128773)))#tab_recordsView | title=Search: species: ''Senecio tamoides'' - Occurrence records}}</ref>
